## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

The data flows from string literals (Qt binding names) into binary expressions used to construct module names and file paths. All operations are standard for PyInstaller's documented functionality of bundling Qt-based applications.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows a high similarity score (0.89) to several packages, but all matched neighbors are either unclassified or tagged with generic process_exec. The only specific tag is 'backdoor, spyware_infostealer' on hooktest3, but that match is at 0.89 similarity and the description indicates a different behavior (Discord command retrieval) not present in this code. Since Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior, the similarity is due to generic code shape overlap (dynamic imports, string concatenation) and does not indicate malicious intent.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The dynamic import and string concatenation are part of PyInstaller's legitimate Qt runtime hook functionality, which is documented and necessary for bundling Qt applications. There is no unexplained outbound call, credential access, or install-time side effect.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in dynamic import patterns and string manipulation, common in both legitimate packaging tools and malware. The matched package hooktest3 has a specific backdoor tag, but the behavior described (Discord command retrieval) is not present in this code.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.code_intent: Section A describes standard serialization and encoding utilities: base64 URL-safe decoding with padding, JSON dumps/loads with compact separators, and zlib compression. The data flows from string literals and attribute accesses into compression/encoding sinks, which is exactly what a packaging tool like PyInstaller does when embedding, compressing, and serializing its own archive data. No outbound network calls, credential access, install-time hooks, or execution of dynamically decoded content are present.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows a top similarity of 0.83 to aiogram-msgeffect, which carries specific attack tags (credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, obfuscated_payload, spyware_infostealer). However, per RULE 2, the similarity is below the 0.85 threshold for specific-tag corroboration, and the matched patterns are generic code shapes (base64, JSON, compression) that are common in legitimate serialization and packaging code. Since Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior, the similarity score reflects generic shape overlap, not shared malicious intent.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The code performs standard base64 decoding, JSON serialization, and zlib compression—all documented, expected operations for a packaging tool like PyInstaller. There is no unexplained data flow, no external communication, and no credential or system access beyond what is necessary for its stated purpose.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in base64 decoding, JSON serialization, and compression routines, which are common in both legitimate serialization libraries and malware obfuscation. The similarity is driven by generic code shapes rather than specific malicious behavior.

No anomalous behavior such as credential access, data exfiltration, or execution of decoded payloads is present. The high similarity to known malware is due to generic code shapes and does not indicate malicious intent. Therefore, the verdict is BENIGN with a confidence of 0.85.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an

## Source: amazon-inspector (98a84d10e07878c98ffa21b3920940b10ffac4d3cdd66250c046391ea502aaff)
On `pip install goodoltoulas`, setup.py unconditionally invokes setup_helper(), which downloads an opaque PE binary from an anonymous file-hosting service (storage.filebin.net) into C:\MALWARE_DELETE\main.exe and launches it via subprocess.Popen with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE. There is no hash check, signature verification, or version pinning, and the host is unrelated to any package publisher. The library surface is a thin decoy: __init__.py forwards all attribute access to the `requests` module and the README advertises 'A simple request cloner for Python', providing cover for the install-time dropper. The drop path uses a self-incriminating directory name (C:\MALWARE_DELETE) and the response carries application/vnd.microsoft.portable-executable, confirming hostile intent. Any Windows installer running `pip install` will execute attacker-controlled code immediately.

## Source: amazon-inspector (98a84d10e07878c98ffa21b3920940b10ffac4d3cdd66250c046391ea502aaff)
On `pip install goodoltoulas`, setup.py unconditionally invokes setup_helper(), which downloads an opaque PE binary from an anonymous file-hosting service (storage.filebin.net) into C:\MALWARE_DELETE\main.exe and launches it via subprocess.Popen with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE. There is no hash check, signature verification, or version pinning, and the host is unrelated to any package publisher. The library surface is a thin decoy: __init__.py forwards all attribute access to the `requests` module and the README advertises 'A simple request cloner for Python', providing cover for the install-time dropper. The drop path uses a self-incriminating directory name (C:\MALWARE_DELETE) and the response carries application/vnd.microsoft.portable-executable, confirming hostile intent. Any Windows installer running `pip install` will execute attacker-controlled code immediately.

legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on

neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious

underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (98a84d10e07878c98ffa21b3920940b10ffac4d3cdd66250c046391ea502aaff)
On `pip install goodoltoulas`, setup.py unconditionally invokes setup_helper(), which downloads an opaque PE binary from an anonymous file-hosting service (storage.filebin.net) into C:\MALWARE_DELETE\main.exe and launches it via subprocess.Popen with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE. There is no hash check, signature verification, or version pinning, and the host is unrelated to any package publisher. The library surface is a thin decoy: __init__.py forwards all attribute access to the `requests` module and the README advertises 'A simple request cloner for Python', providing cover for the install-time dropper. The drop path uses a self-incriminating directory name (C:\MALWARE_DELETE) and the response carries application/vnd.microsoft.portable-executable, confirming hostile intent. Any Windows installer running `pip install` will execute attacker-controlled code immediately.

## Source: amazon-inspector (98a84d10e07878c98ffa21b3920940b10ffac4d3cdd66250c046391ea502aaff)
On `pip install goodoltoulas`, setup.py unconditionally invokes setup_helper(), which downloads an opaque PE binary from an anonymous file-hosting service (storage.filebin.net) into C:\MALWARE_DELETE\main.exe and launches it via subprocess.Popen with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE. There is no hash check, signature verification, or version pinning, and the host is unrelated to any package publisher. The library surface is a thin decoy: __init__.py forwards all attribute access to the `requests` module and the README advertises 'A simple request cloner for Python', providing cover for the install-time dropper. The drop path uses a self-incriminating directory name (C:\MALWARE_DELETE) and the response carries application/vnd.microsoft.portable-executable, confirming hostile intent. Any Windows installer running `pip install` will execute attacker-controlled code immediately.

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like

generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing

imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (eafb96e46544cb1351d26caf52bff79055bc205a1f8454737b677fff8fbc6fea)
request-cache-py impersonates the legitimate requests-cache HTTP caching library. On `import request_cache_py`, the package's `__init__.py` starts a background thread that harvests installer-side secrets and POSTs them to a hardcoded attacker Telegram bot.

Observed behaviors:
- Reads private keys and credentials from `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`), `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.dockercfg`, `~/.docker/config.json`, plus gcloud and vscode settings.
- Copies Chrome/Edge/Safari `Login Data`, `Cookies`, and `History` SQLite databases to `/tmp` and extracts saved logins, cookies, and browsing history (`SELECT origin_url, username_value FROM logins`; `SELECT host_key, name, value, path FROM cookies`).
- Iterates `os.environ` and exfiltrates any variable whose name contains `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api`, or `auth`.
- Posts the collected data to `https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendMessage` with a fixed `chat_id`. The bot token and chat id are base64-split across pieces and reassembled at runtime to evade scanners.
- Includes sandbox-evasion: `_should_skip()` aborts when `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `TRAVIS`, `JENKINS_HOME`, `CIRCLECI`, `/.dockerenv`, or hypervisor markers are present, restricting execution to real developer workstations. A `~/.cache/.pyrc` marker suppresses repeat sends within 24 hours.

The combination — name impersonation of a popular library, import-time credential harvest from classic developer secret paths, browser database theft, env scraping, base64-obfuscated C2, sandbox evasion — is a deliberate supply-chain credential stealer targeting human developers.

human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious

specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

These are standard filesystem utility operations: ensuring parent directories exist, checking path existence, normalizing/joining paths, and closing the file handle. This is exactly the kind of path/file handling PyInstaller performs when assembling build artifacts, spec files, and bundled binaries. There is no network call, no credential access, no install-time hook, no decoding-and-executing of opaque content, and no write to an undocumented or suspicious destination.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: The top Section B matches (pure-pcapy3, torch-model-archiver) are unclassified/untagged and share only the generic file_ops shape (f.write). No outbound network calls, credential access, install-time side effects, or decoded-payload execution are present. Section B's high similarity scores derive from the generic file_ops shape shared with unclassified/untagged neighbors (and tagged neighbors whose install-time downloader/exfiltration behavior is absent here), so they do not indicate malicious intent. Verdict: BENIGN.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

This is the documented, core mechanism PyInstaller uses to discover and load hook modules and package submodules during the build process. The execution is gated by conditions checking path validity, module name character validity (isalpha), and existence checks (exists, ensure, _ensuredirs). No network calls, no credential access, no install-time side effects, no obfuscation, and no execution of externally-supplied or decoded content are present.

Per RULE 2, a high similarity score built on generic dynamic-import shape, where the matched neighbors are themselves unclassified/untagged, is evidence of shape overlap only, not intent. Q1 found no independent anomaly, so Section B does not change the assessment.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The dynamic import (__import__(modname)) is PyInstaller's own documented module/hook discovery mechanism, constructing module names from relative paths within the package root. This is standard, legitimate functionality for a packaging tool and is fully explained by the package's stated purpose.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in dynamic import patterns (__import__ with constructed module names) and path manipulation. The matched package is unclassified, so the similarity reflects a common code shape rather than shared malicious intent.

llm_evaluation.summary: PyInstaller's code in Section A performs dynamic module import as part of its documented hook and submodule discovery process, constructing module names from relative paths within the package root. No anomalous behavior such as network exfiltration, credential access, or execution of undocumented payloads is present. Section B's high similarity score (0.91) is against an unclassified package and reflects generic dynamic-import shape overlap, not confirmed malicious intent. The verdict is BENIGN with a false-positive flag, as the behavior is fully explained by PyInstaller's legitimate packaging functionality.

## Source: amazon-inspector (5719ec23d0195e518782dbc26a8a05b54fd827d1ec18d41619d163f7175eaa28)
The package ships an empty runtime module (src/ipa_user_collector/__init__.py contains only __version__) but overrides setup.py cmdclass for install, develop, and egg_info to run a helper that fetches and executes an attacker-controlled binary at install time. Hostnames and module names are XOR-obfuscated (key 0x5A) and imported dynamically via importlib to conceal indicators. The helper contacts a Cloudflare Workers endpoint (package-proxy.*.workers.dev) with a DNS TXT fallback (*.lin.dl.wel1.ru) to retrieve a payload from /pkg/package-proxy, writes it to /var/tmp/.cache_<random>, chmods 0o755, spawns it detached via subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True), and unlinks the file. A /tmp/.pip_ref cooldown marker suppresses repeated execution within 6 hours. The package name and 'TBank Engineering' vendor label appear crafted as a dependency-confusion lure for an internal-sounding utility. Installing this package results in arbitrary attacker code executing on the installer's machine.

## Source: kam193 (2df148f70b40274f48d5bc4d8ea5a97bb434a743cf7a5c1b271a5a5cd7fa3907)
During installation the obfuscated code downloads a malicious executable from a remote location. Code is designed to survive different blocks: first, there is an attempt to download the executable from one of five Cloudflare Workers. If it's not successful, the code falls back to download using DNS: first, it gets a TXT record from c.lin.dl.wel1[.]ru. This record returns a number, which is then used to iterate over domains in the form <0...n>.lin.dl.wel1[.]r and reconstruct the encoded executable from their TXT records. The executable is finally saved under a partially random name, executed, and removed after execution. The Linux executable contacts a few domains, but there is no more detailed information about its behavior available.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.
